t: Examination of a newborn's body: situations and questions
n: In this topic we consider the examination of a newborn's body. Examination is ordered when there are signs of violent death or suspicion of it. For example, when the body of a newborn with an unknown mother is found, in stillbirth outside a medical institution, or when a complaint about care is received. In such a case, special questions are put: whether the infant is newborn, whether it was born alive, what its gestational age is, whether it was viable, how long it lived, and whether it was cared for. At the same time, as usual, the cause and time of death, bodily injuries and their mechanism are determined.

First, let us define the concept of a newborn. In forensic medicine the newborn period is taken as the first 24 hours. In paediatrics this period is 4 weeks, that is, the neonatal period, and in obstetrics and gynaecology 7 days. Now the legal aspect. In the Criminal Code, the deliberate killing of a child by its mother during birth or immediately after birth is singled out, this is Article 99. Its penalty is more lenient than that for deliberate murder. If other persons commit the same act, it is classed as deliberate murder, that is, Article 97.

Let us consider the first group of signs of being newborn. Traces of blood on the infant's body arise from rupture of the soft tissues of the birth canal and disappear on washing. Vernix caseosa may persist for up to a week. The caput succedaneum is located on the head, sometimes the buttocks, is soft and is absorbed in 2–3 days; it is also found across the projection of the sutures. A cephalohaematoma is different: it is haemorrhage under the periosteum. It lies over a bone, is limited by the sutures and is absorbed over 2 weeks or more.

t: Signs of being newborn (II): meconium and umbilical cord
n: The second group of signs concerns meconium and the umbilical cord. Meconium is a dark green semi-liquid mass, usually passed within 1–2 days, and in premature infants up to 3–4 days. In full-term infants the umbilical cord is 50–60 cm long and 1.5–2 cm thick; it is moist and shiny, and shrivels on drying. In those born alive, a demarcation ring appears at the base of the cord after several hours, sometimes at the end of the first day. Then after 5–7 days the cord falls off. That is, these signs give a consistent dynamic in assessing how long the infant lived.

Now let us distinguish absolute and relative signs. Primary atelectasis of the lungs means that the infant did not breathe; such an infant may have lived several seconds. There are three absolutely reliable signs: primary atelectasis of the lungs, absence of the demarcation ring or its initial signs, and a cord not separated from the body and placenta. The other signs are relative. They may also be found on the second and subsequent days of life. Remember: traces of blood and vernix caseosa are among the relative signs.

t: Live birth and the lung test
n: We turn to the question of live birth. By WHO criteria, outside the mother's body the infant must show breathing, heartbeat, umbilical cord pulsation or voluntary movement. Methods of determining heartbeat and movement after death have not been developed. Therefore the question is resolved mainly by whether the infant breathed or not. For this the lung test is used, that is, the Galen–Rauger–Schreyer test; Schreyer proposed it in 1681. The specific gravity of a lung that has not breathed is 1.05–1.06, and of one that has breathed, below 1.0.

Errors are possible in the lung test. A false positive result is obtained in a putrefied body, after artificial respiration, and in frozen lungs not fully thawed. A false negative result occurs in secondary atelectasis. In such a case the Taranukhin method, 1907, or the Trakhtenberg modification, 1958, is recommended. In the Taranukhin method, a piece of lung floats up in a flask of water under reduced pressure. This means that the result of the test must always be evaluated together with the condition of the body.

Another method is the gastrointestinal test, that is, the Breslau test, 1865. When an infant breathes, air passes into the gastrointestinal tract. Therefore ligatures are placed, the gastrointestinal tract is put in water, and the parts containing air float. The gradual passage of air is also used to determine how long the infant lived. However, in putrefaction and artificial ventilation this test gives a false positive. The radiological test, Dillon, 1939, is no longer used.

Now let us compare the macroscopic and microscopic signs. In those born alive the chest is barrel-shaped and the diaphragm stands at the level of the 6th–7th rib. In stillborns the chest is flat and the diaphragm is at the level of the 4th–5th rib. Lung weight is 55–60 g if no breathing occurred and 85–90 g after breathing, and the surface is marbled, which is the Bush–Haberda sign. Under the microscope, in a lung that has breathed the alveoli are expanded and the epithelium is flat. If no breathing occurred, the alveoli are not expanded and the epithelium is cuboidal.

t: Hyaline membranes and basics of gestational age
n: Hyaline membranes are found in those who lived several hours, mainly in premature infants; they are absent from lungs that have not breathed. Now the basics of gestational age. Full term means that the pregnancy lasted on average 10 months, or 280 days. By WHO, delivery at 37–42 weeks is regarded as on time. In full-term infants body length is 50–54 cm and weight 3000–3500 g. For a mature fetus, body length must be 45 cm or more and weight not less than 2500 g.

There are several ways to calculate gestational age. In Haase's method, in the first half of pregnancy the square root of the body length is taken, and in the second half the length is divided by 5. For example, 16 cm is 4 months, and 40 cm is 8 months. The Balthazard–Dervieux index is 5.6: 40 cm × 5.6 = 224 days, that is, 8 months. Yakupov, 1981, proposed dividing the head circumference by 3.4; 34 cm is 10 months. There is also a table by cord length and placental mass, table 10.1. In it, for example, for X months the values 50 — 500 are given.

We also assess gestational age by ossification centres. In the calcaneus the centre appears in the 5th month, in the talus in the 7th month, and in the lower femoral epiphysis, that is, the Béclard nucleus, in the 9th month. Pathology of pregnancy, smoking, alcohol and drugs may delay the appearance of the centres. Now viability. By WHO, an infant shorter than 25 cm and lighter than 500 g is considered non-viable. Malformations such as anencephaly and a two-chambered heart also preclude viability.

We assess how long the infant lived from several signs. The demarcation ring appears at the end of the first day. The passage of meconium also falls in this period, and the caput succedaneum is absorbed in 2–3 days. For hyaline membranes to form, at least 1–2 hours of life are needed, and for secondary atelectasis at least 5–6 hours. If air is only in the stomach, the infant lived less than 3 hours. At 5–6 hours air reaches the small intestine, and after 6 hours it passes into the large intestine.

t: Signs of care and causes of death
n: Now the signs of care and causes of death. Care looks like this: the infant is swaddled and dressed, the cord is cut and tied, the infant is cleaned of blood and vernix caseosa, and there is milk in the stomach. As for causes of death, in antenatal non-violent death the cause is placenta praevia, infarction, abruption, cord compression or a true knot. Therefore the placenta and cord are examined too. The cause of intranatal death is mainly birth trauma, that is, injury of the parietal and frontal bones; no external injuries or wounds are formed.

t: Violent death and injury inflicted by the woman
n: One kind of violent death is injury inflicted by the woman giving birth. If the woman injures the fetus with her hand, abrasions, bruises and tears of the corners of the mouth arise on the face and neck. Violent death occurs mainly in the postnatal period. Active methods include strangulation, closing the respiratory openings, drowning, compression, mechanical injury and throwing into fire. The passive method is abandonment without care, which, if the cord is not tied, leads to external bleeding, freezing and starvation. The legal significance is that the exact cause of death must be stated.

t: Features of examining a newborn's body
n: Examination of a newborn's body has its own features. In external examination, anthropometry, traces of blood, vernix caseosa, fontanelles, firmness of the ear and nasal cartilage, nail length and meconium staining are assessed. Internal examination begins with the chest and abdomen. To study the oral cavity and palate, the midline incision begins not from the chin but from the lower lip. Windows are opened in the cranial vault. For histological and forensic biological examination, pieces of the internal organs, placenta and cord are taken.

Now we move on to asphyxia and first consider the types of hypoxia. Cessation of tissue respiration in the central nervous system leads to irreversible changes in 5–10 minutes. Exogenous hypoxia is of three kinds: hypoxic, hyperoxic and hypercapnic. Endogenous hypoxia is divided into respiratory, haemic, circulatory, cytotoxic and physiological. By rate of development, fulminant, that is, seconds, acute, that is, minutes, subacute, that is, hours, and chronic hypoxia are distinguished. For forensic medicine the fulminant and acute types are significant.

Asphyxia is an acute disturbance of the functioning of vital systems resulting from oxygen deficiency and accumulation of carbon dioxide due to impaired external respiration. There are three types of mechanical asphyxia. The first is from compression: strangulation and compression asphyxia. The second is from obstruction: obstruction of the respiratory openings, obstruction of the airways, and drowning. The third is asphyxia in a confined space. A special case is autoerotic asphyxiation, in which sexual arousal arises under conditions of hypoxia. If this ends in death, it is regarded as an accident.

Asphyxia passes through several periods. The preasphyxial period lasts on average 20–30 seconds; the organism compensates and no signs develop. Then inspiratory dyspnoea begins: breathing quickens, consciousness is lost in 40–60 seconds, the period lasting about a minute. After it comes expiratory dyspnoea. In it there are strong clonic convulsions, and urine, semen and faeces are passed; this too lasts about a minute. After that come the periods of brief respiratory arrest, terminal breathing and complete arrest.

t: Periods of asphyxia (II) and cardiac arrest
n: Let us consider the continuation of the periods. Brief respiratory arrest lasts 30–40 seconds. Terminal breathing lasts up to 5 minutes. After breathing stops completely, the heart may go on beating for another 3–10 minutes. N. Minovici in 1905 conducted an experiment on himself with hanging. Reflex cardiac arrest arises from irritation of the receptors of the carotid sinus, larynx and trachea. If this arrest lasts up to 30 seconds, the general asphyxial signs do not develop. Remember: in such a death the signs of asphyxia may be absent.

When the asphyxial insult ends without death, for example in a rescued drowning person or one cut down from hanging, a postasphyxial state develops. It consists of 4 periods. The first is asphyxial coma, the second stupor, the third disorientation and memory disturbance, and the fourth residual effects. In the first day, death occurs from pulmonary and cerebral oedema. Later, death may occur from hypostatic pneumonia. In the first hours, pulmonary oedema is considered an unfavourable sign.

Let us list the general external signs of asphyxia. Cyanosis of the face and neck is not constant: lying on the back it may disappear, while lying face down it may be present in other circumstances too. Extensive bluish-violet cadaveric lividity appears quickly, within an hour; petechial haemorrhages may also be present. Subconjunctival ecchymoses, inconstant pupillary dilatation, and involuntary passage of urine and faeces are also observed. None of these signs alone gives a definite diagnosis.

Now the general internal signs. The heart and large veins contain dark red fluid blood. The right chambers of the heart are fuller than the left, which is called the asphyxial heart. Venous congestion is found in the internal organs, and partial emphysema in the lungs. Tardieu spots are dark red haemorrhages 2–3 mm in size under the visceral pleura and epicardium. There is also an anaemic, shrunken spleen, which is Sabinsky's sign. The set of these signs is called the general asphyxial signs.

Let us consider hanging. Strangulation asphyxia accounts for more than two thirds of deaths from mechanical asphyxia, and hanging for 65–70 %. In hanging, the neck organs are compressed by a ligature under the weight of the body or part of it. In most cases it is a method of suicide. In typical, that is, complete hanging, the body hangs freely. In atypical, that is, incomplete hanging, part of the body has support. In typical hanging the knot lies at the back, in atypical hanging at the front or side.

By material, the ligature is divided into three types. Soft ligature: towel, scarf, tie. Semi-rigid: rope, belt. Rigid: wire, chain. The ligature may have one, two or many turns. The knot has criminalistic significance. Therefore the ligature is cut on the side opposite the knot, and the knot is not disturbed. If the knot is at the back, the position is called typical; if at the front or side, atypical.

Death in hanging occurs by several mechanisms. First, the airway narrows because the base of the tongue is displaced; sometimes the airway is completely closed. Second, the jugular veins are compressed, intracranial pressure rises and brain function is disturbed. Third, irritation of the vagus and superior laryngeal nerves and of the carotid sinus may lead to reflex cardiac arrest. With an atypical knot, vomiting and aspiration may also occur.

The main sign of hanging is the strangulation furrow on the neck in the form of an abrasion. A furrow made by a semi-rigid ligature persists for 10–15 days. In typical hanging the furrow lies high, above the hyoid bone, and is obliquely vertical; in atypical hanging it is lower. A rigid ligature leaves a firmer and deeper furrow. With a soft ligature no skin furrow is visible, but internally the "copper wire sign", that is, Casper's sign, is found.

Additional signs are also found in hanging. In anisocoria the pupil is wider on the side of greater constriction. Injury of the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage is not characteristic of hanging. Haemorrhage behind the larynx is called Brouardel's sign. There are also signs of stretching: rupture of the intima of the carotid artery, that is, Amussat's sign, and also the signs of Martin, Walcher and Simon. They occur mainly in typical hanging with a jerk in obese people.

The question whether the furrow was inflicted during life is important. A skin flap is cleared of fat and examined between two glass slides against the light. Congestion and haemorrhage in the ridge are considered a sign of vitality, which is the Bocarius test. Under the microscope, circulatory disturbance, that is, Neiding's sign, and reactive inflammation, that is, Kasyanov's sign, are seen. These signs confirm that the furrow was inflicted during life.

Ligature strangulation differs from hanging. Here the ligature is tightened not by the weight of the body but by an outside force. In most cases it is homicide. The reflexogenic zones are irritated more, so death may result from reflex cardiac arrest before the signs of asphyxia have fully developed. The furrow is horizontal, lies at the level of the thyroid cartilage or lower, and is often continuous. Injury of the hyoid bone is not characteristic. Signs of struggle may be present. In hanging, by contrast, the furrow is obliquely vertical, interrupted, and broken at the site of the knot.

Manual strangulation is usually homicide. Finger marks take the form of round or oval bruises, over which arc-shaped abrasions from fingernails are found. Internal injuries are more pronounced than external ones: the hyoid bone and the thyroid, cricoid and tracheal cartilages are fractured, and haemorrhage occurs into the neck tissues. Positional asphyxia results from remaining for a long time with the head flexed. In it there is no furrow, and the hyoid bone and cartilages are not injured. The diagnosis rests on excluding other causes.

t: Obstructive asphyxia: respiratory openings and airways
n: The first form of obstructive asphyxia is obstruction of the respiratory openings. Closing the respiratory openings with a hand or soft object occurs in young children or in weakened adults. If there was no resistance, there is no specific sign. If there was resistance, there may be bruises and abrasions around the mouth and nose, haemorrhages in the mucosa of the mouth and gums, and superficial wounds. The airways may be obstructed by foreign bodies: a fruit stone, button, toy, dentures, and also pourable substances, blood and vomit. This is mostly an accident.

Let us dwell on the causes of airway obstruction. Alcohol and drug intoxication and craniocerebral injury impair the swallowing and cough reflexes. In nasopharyngeal bleeding and fracture of the skull base, blood is aspirated. Vomit has an acid reaction, is more aggressive than blood and causes chemical injury to the bronchi and alveoli. In resuscitation, transportation and putrefaction, the mass that enters the airways is small and is not found in the small bronchi and alveoli. Therefore histology is necessary.

Drowning takes second place after hanging among deaths from mechanical asphyxia. More than 300 thousand deaths a year are recorded worldwide. Types of drowning: true, that is, aspiration or "wet"; asphyxial, that is, spastic or "dry"; and mixed. In asphyxial drowning, water does not enter the trachea and bronchi because of laryngeal spasm. True drowning occurs in the warm season, in warm water and in intoxicated persons. Asphyxial drowning is seen with severe stress, in cold water and in young children.

Let us consider the signs of true drowning. Around the mouth and nose there is persistent white fine-bubbled froth, which is Krushevsky's sign. The lungs are doughy, enlarged and "marbled". Rasskazov–Lukomsky–Paltauf spots lie under the visceral pleura and not under the epicardium. The blood of the left heart is paler, which is Casper's sign. The abdominal cavity contains about 100 ml of fluid, which is Morro's sign. Up to 300 ml of water is found in the stomach, which is Fegerlund's sign. Haemorrhages in the muscles are Paltauf's sign.

In asphyxial drowning there is no water in the airways, and the lungs are dry and emphysematous; only Tardieu spots are found. The stomach may contain up to 1 l of water, and 5–15 ml of fluid is found at the skull base, which is Sveshnikov's sign. Air embolism of the heart and lymphohaemia are also examined. In the Sunsov test the left ventricle is punctured. To determine vitality, diatom plankton is examined: in parenchymatous organs and bone marrow, 15–50 µm in size. Pseudoplankton, bacteriological and cryoscopic methods are also used. Diatoms in the lungs are not diagnostic.

t: Signs of a body's immersion in water
n: Let us consider the signs of a body having been in water. The body cools faster. The skin pales and "goose skin" appears. After several hours the fingers turn pale and wrinkle. On days 2–5 the palm changes, on days 5–8 the sole; this is the "washerwoman's hand". After 2–3 weeks the skin separates in the form of a "glove of death", and after 10–15 days the hair is easily pulled out. The higher the temperature, the faster the changes proceed. In newborns the vernix caseosa protects against maceration. These signs do not depend on the cause of death.

In compression asphyxia the movement of the chest and abdomen is restricted. It occurs in natural and man-made disasters and in crowd crushes; frontal compression is more dangerous than lateral. Signs: swelling and blueness of the face, an "ecchymotic mask" on the face, neck and chest, that is, the Olive–Danger sign, and "carmine swelling" of the lungs, that is, Lacassagne's sign. In a confined space, breathing quickens at 0.5 % carbon dioxide. Life-threatening levels are 8–10 % in adults and 2.0–2.5 % in children. There are no specific signs.
